      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Bacterial</span> Infections</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Flesh-Eating <span class="qt1">Bacteria</span></content>

      <content name="FullSummary">What are <span class="qt1">bacteria</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Bacteria</span> are tiny organisms (living things) that have only one cell. Under a microscope, they look like balls, rods, or spirals. They can be found almost everywhere on Earth. There are lots of <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> in and on your body. In fact, your body has about 10 times more <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> cells than human cells.</p><p>There are many different types of <span class="qt1">bacteria</span>. Most types don't make you sick. Some types are helpful. For example, "good" <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> in your digestive system can help your body digest food and absorb vitamins and minerals. They can help protect you from getting sick. <span class="qt1">Bacteria</span> are also used in making foods like yogurt and cheese.</p><p>But some types of <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> can cause an infection and make you sick. They are called infectious <span class="qt1">bacteria. These bacteria</span> can reproduce quickly in your body. Many of them give off toxins (poisons) that can damage your cells and make you sick. Other types can move into and damage your tissues. A few examples of <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> that cause infections include Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, and E. coli.</p>How do <span class="qt1">bacterial</span> infections spread?<p>There are different ways that <span class="qt1">bacterial</span> infections may spread:</p><ul><li>Through droplets and particles that are breathed out by someone who has the infection. You might breathe in the droplets or particles, or they could land on your mouth, nose, or eyes. 
</li><li>By touching surfaces or objects that have the <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> on them and then touching your mouth, nose, or eyes.</li><li>Through cuts, scrapes, and skin-to-skin contact with someone who has the infection.</li><li>From the pregnant parent to the baby during pregnancy.</li><li>Through contaminated food or water.</li><li>By being bitten by an infected insect or animal.</li><li>Through sexual contact (usually vaginal, anal and oral sex) with someone who has the infection.</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt1">bacterial</span> infections?<p>Sometimes your immune system may be able to fight off a <span class="qt1">bacterial</span> infection. But when you do need treatment, it will be with antibiotics.</p><p></p>antibiotic resistance<p></p>Can <span class="qt1">bacterial</span> infections be prevented?<p>You can help prevent some <span class="qt1">bacterial</span> infections by:</p><ul><li>Getting vaccines that protect against <span class="qt1">bacterial</span> infections.</li><li>Having good hygiene habits. These include washing your hands often and covering your mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing.</li><li>Paying attention to food safety.</li><li>Cleaning and disinfecting surfaces that your frequently touch.</li><li>Preventing insect bites by using a U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)-registered insect repellent. when you go outdoors. If you travel to an area that has a high risk of diseases from insect bites, also wear long pants, shirts, and socks.</li><li>Practicing safe sex. This means using a latex condom every time you have anal, vaginal, or oral sex. If your or your partner is allergic to latex, you can use polyurethane condoms.</li><li>Avoiding close contact with people who are sick.</li></ul></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/antibioticresistance.html">
      <content name="title">Antibiotic Resistance</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Antimicrobial Resistance</content>
      <content name="altTitle">VRE</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Vancomycin-Resistant Enterococci</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Vancomycin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are antibiotics?<p>Antibiotics are medicines that treat <span class="qt1">bacterial</span> infections in humans and animals. They work by killing the <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> or making it hard for the <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> to grow and multiply. When used properly, antibiotics can save lives. But there is a growing problem of antibiotic resistance.</p>What is antibiotic resistance?<p>Antibiotic resistance happens when <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> change and can resist the effects of an antibiotic. The <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> are not killed, and they continue to grow. The infections these <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> cause are called resistant infections. Resistant infections can be difficult, and sometimes impossible, to treat. In some cases, they can even be deadly. </p><p>Antibiotic resistance does not mean that your body is resistant to antibiotics.</p><p>There are many different types of resistant infections. They include MRSA and drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB). If you get a resistant infection, you might need:</p><ul><li>A long hospital stay</li><li>A long recovery</li><li>Follow-up visits with health care providers</li><li>Treatments that are expensive and may have severe side effects</li></ul><p>Antibiotic resistance is one type of antimicrobial resistance. There are other types; viruses, fungi, and parasites can also become resistant to medicines.</p>How do <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> become resistant to antibiotics?<p>Antibiotic resistance is a natural process that happens over time. To survive, <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> can develop defense strategies against antibiotics. This happens through genetic changes in the <span class="qt1">bacteria</span>. These resistant <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> survive, grow, and spread.</p><p>Each time you take antibiotics, there is a risk that the <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> will become resistant. So it is important to only take antibiotics when you really need them. They won't work on viral infections such as colds and the flu. And you don't need antibiotics for every <span class="qt1">bacterial</span> infection. For example, you may not need them for some sinus and ear infections.</p>Who is more likely to develop an antibiotic-resistant infection?<p>Anyone can develop an antibiotic-resistant infection, but certain people may be at higher risk, including those who:</p><ul><li>Have a weakened immune system from diseases such as HIV or from taking medicines that affect the immune system</li><li>Are getting medical care such as surgery and hospital stays</li><li>Take antibiotics for a long time</li><li>Are infants, especially if they were born prematurely</li><li>Are older adults</li></ul>How can antibiotic resistance be prevented?<p>There will always be some antibiotic resistance, since it happens naturally. But you can help fight against antibiotic resistance by taking these steps:</p><ul><li>Don't use antibiotics for viruses.</li><li>Don't pressure your health care provider to give you an antibiotic if they don't think you need one.</li><li>When you take antibiotics, follow the directions carefully.</li><li>Don't share your antibiotics with others.</li><li>Don't save antibiotics for later or use someone else's prescription.</li><li>Help prevent the spread of <span class="qt1">bacterial</span> infections with good hygiene habits. These include washing your hands often and covering your mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing.</li></ul><p>Centers for Disease Control and Prevention</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/meningococcaldisease.html">
      <content name="title">Meningococcal Disease</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Meningococcal Infections</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Meningococcemia</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is meningococcal disease?<p>Meningococcal disease is the name for any illness that is caused by Neisseria meningitidis <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> (also called meningococcal <span class="qt1">bacteria</span>). These illnesses are often severe and can sometimes be deadly. They include infections of the lining of the brain and spinal cord (meningitis) and in the bloodstream (sepsis). Vaccines can help prevent the disease.</p>What causes meningococcal disease?<p>Some people have Neisseria meningitidis, the <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> that cause the disease, in the back of their nose and throat. They usually have the <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> but don't get sick. This is called being a "carrier." But sometimes the <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> can spread to other parts of the body and cause meningococcal disease.</p><p>The <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> can spread from person to person through saliva (spit). It usually happens through close or lengthy contact with a person who has it. Close contact can include things like kissing and coughing.</p><p>You cannot catch the <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> through casual contact with someone who has the disease. For example, you cannot get it by breathing air where that person has been.</p>Who is more likely to get meningococcal disease?<p>Anyone can get meningococcal disease, but you are more likely to get it if someone you live with has it. You are also more likely to get it if you have direct contact with the saliva of someone who has it (like through kissing).</p><p>Also, certain groups of people are more likely to get the disease. They include:</p><ul><li>Children younger than 1 year old.</li><li>Teens and young adults ages 16 through 23 years old.</li><li>Adults 65 years and older.</li><li>People with medical conditions that weaken their immune system, including those with HIV and certain rare immune system diseases.</li><li>People who either don't have a spleen or have a spleen that does not function well.</li><li>People who take complement inhibitor. These are immunotherapy medicines that are given to people with certain rare conditions.</li><li>People who live in crowded settings, such as college dorms or military barracks.</li><li>People who travel to areas where the disease is more common, such as certain parts of sub-Saharan Africa.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of meningococcal disease?<p>There are different types of meningococcal disease. The most common types are meningitis and septicemia. Both types are very serious and can be deadly in a matter of hours.</p><p>Meningococcal meningitis is a meningococcal infection of the lining of the brain and spinal cord. The most common symptoms include:</p><ul><li>Fever</li><li>Headache</li><li>Stiff neck</li></ul><p>It can also cause symptoms such as:</p><ul><li>Nausea and vomiting</li><li>Photophobia (your eyes being more sensitive to light)</li><li>Confusion</li></ul><p>It may be hard to notice these symptoms in newborns and babies. They can also have different symptoms. They may:</p><ul><li>Be slow or inactive</li><li>Be irritable</li><li>Vomit</li><li>Feed poorly</li><li>Have a bulging of the soft spot of their skull</li></ul><p>Meningococcal septicemia is a meningococcal infection of the bloodstream. It's also called meningococcemia. When someone has this disease, the <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> enter the bloodstream and multiply. This damages the walls of the blood vessels and causes bleeding into the skin and organs. The symptoms may include:</p><ul><li>Fever and chills</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Vomiting</li><li>Cold hands and feet</li><li>Severe aches or pain in the muscles, joints, chest, or abdomen (belly)</li><li>Rapid breathing</li><li>Diarrhea</li><li>A dark purple rash (in the later stages of the disease)</li></ul><p>Because it is so serious, you need to seek immediate medical attention if you or your child develops the symptoms of meningococcal disease.</p>How is meningococcal disease diagnosed?<p>The signs and symptoms of meningococcal disease are often similar to those of other illnesses. This can make it hard to diagnose.</p><p>If your (or your child's) health care provider thinks that you or your child could have meningococcal disease, they will order tests that take samples of blood and/or cerebrospinal fluid  (fluid near the spinal cord). They will send the samples to a lab for testing. The testing will include <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> culture testing, which can identify the specific type of <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> that is causing the infection. Knowing this can help the provider decide on the best treatment.</p>What are the treatments for meningococcal disease?<p>Certain antibiotics can treat meningococcal disease. It is important that treatment is started as soon as possible. So if the provider thinks you have meningococcal disease, they will give you antibiotics right away (before the test results come back).</p><p>People with serious disease may need additional treatments, such as:</p><ul><li>Breathing support</li><li>Medicines to treat low blood pressure</li><li>Surgery to remove dead tissue</li><li>Wound care for parts of the body with damaged skin</li></ul><p>Some people with meningococcal disease will have long-term health problems and disabilities. These may include:</p><ul><li>Loss of limb(s)</li><li>Deafness</li><li>Nervous system problems</li><li>Brain damage</li></ul><p>Even with treatment, 10 to 15 in 100 people will die from the disease.</p>Can meningococcal disease be prevented?<p>The best way to prevent meningococcal disease is to get vaccinated. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends meningococcal vaccination for:</p><ul><li>All preteens and teens</li><li>Children at higher risk for meningococcal disease</li><li>Adults at higher risk for meningococcal disease</li></ul><p>If you are a close contact of a person with meningococcal disease, you will likely be given antibiotics to prevent you from getting sick. This is called "prophylaxis."  Close contacts include people who are living together. They also include people who had direct contact with the saliva of a person who has the disease (such as from kissing).</p><p>Although it's rare, you can get meningococcal disease more than once.</p><p>Centers for Disease Control and Prevention</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/legionnairesdisease.html">
      <content name="title">Legionnaires' Disease</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Legionellosis</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is Legionnaires' Disease? <p>Legionnaires' disease is a serious type of pneumonia caused by Legionella <span class="qt1">bacteria</span>. The disease got its name when a group of people at an American Legion convention became ill with this type of pneumonia.</p><p>Legionella is found naturally in freshwater, such as lakes and rivers. It can also be found in soil. But people usually only get sick from it when if it grows and spreads in man-made water systems. These systems can include hot tubs, fountains, and the plumbing systems of large buildings, such as hotels or nursing homes.</p><p>Legionella can also cause Pontiac fever. This is a milder, flu-like illness that doesn't infect your lungs.</p><p></p>What causes Legionnaires' disease?<p></p><p>You usually can't get infected by drinking water that contains the <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> unless you aspirate it (accidentally breathe the water into your lungs). The <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> don't spread from person to person. Disease outbreaks happen when many people are exposed to the same water source that contains the <span class="qt1">bacteria</span>.</p>Who is more likely to develop Legionnaires' disease?<p>Most healthy people who come in contact with the <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> do not become sick. You are more likely to develop an infection if you:</p><ul><li>Are over the age of 50</li><li>Are a current or former smoker</li><li>Have a chronic (long-lasting) disease such as diabetes or kidney failure</li><li>Have a chronic lung disease such as COPD or emphysema</li><li>Have a weakened immune system due to a disease such as HIV or cancer or are taking medicines that suppress your immune system</li><li>Live in a long-term care facility</li><li>Have recently stayed in a hospital or had surgery requiring anesthesia</li></ul>What are the symptoms of Legionnaires' disease? <p>The symptoms usually show up 2 to 14 days after you were exposed to Legionella <span class="qt1">bacteria</span>. Most of the symptoms are similar to those of other types of pneumonia. But Legionnaires' disease may also cause gastrointestinal symptoms and mental changes.</p><p>The symptoms of Legionnaires' disease may include:</p><ul><li>Cough</li><li>High fever</li><li>Chills</li><li>Headache</li><li>Chest pain</li><li>Shortness of breath</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Nausea and vomiting</li><li>Diarrhea</li><li>Confusion</li></ul>What other problems can Legionnaires' disease cause?<p>Legionnaires' disease can cause life-threatening complications such as respiratory failure, kidney failure, and sepsis.</p><p>About 1 out of every 10 people who get sick with Legionnaires' disease will die from complications of the illness.</p>How is Legionnaires' disease diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have Legionnaires' disease, your health care provider will probably order a chest x-ray to see if you have pneumonia. If you do have it, lab tests such as a urine or sputum test can check for the Legionella <span class="qt1">bacteria</span>. Your provider may also order a blood test to see if you have been exposed to the <span class="qt1">bacteria</span>.</p>What are the treatments for Legionnaires' disease?<p>If you have Legionnaires' disease, you will likely need care in a hospital. The treatment is with antibiotics. Most people will recover, especially if they were healthy when they got the disease. Getting treatment early can increase the chances of getting better.</p>Can Legionnaires' disease be prevented?<p>You can lower your risk of getting Legionnaires' disease if you:</p><ul><li>Clean all your water-related devices regularly. This could include portable humidifiers, water heaters, air conditioners, and nasal rinses.</li><li>If you haven't used your faucets and showerheads for a week or more, flush them by letting the hot and cold faucets run for at least two minutes before use.</li><li>Avoid exposure to water sources such as decorative foundations or hot tubs if you don't know how well they are maintained.</li><li>Use windshield cleaner in your wiper fluid tank in your car instead of water.</li><li>Ask about how well your buildings' water systems are maintained.</li></ul><p>Centers for Disease Control and Prevention</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/antibiotics.html">
      <content name="title">Antibiotics</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are antibiotics?<p>Antibiotics are medicines that fight <span class="qt1">bacterial</span> infections in people and animals. They work by killing the <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> or by making it hard for the <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> to grow and multiply.</p><p>Antibiotics can be taken in different ways:</p><ul><li>Orally (by mouth). This could be pills, capsules, or liquids.</li><li>Topically. This might be a cream, spray, or ointment that you put on your skin. It could also be eye ointment, eye drops, or ear drops.</li><li>Through an injection or intravenously (IV). This is usually for more serious infections.</li></ul>What do antibiotics treat?<p>Antibiotics only treat certain <span class="qt1">bacterial</span> infections, such as strep throat, urinary tract infections, and E. coli.</p><p>You may not need to take antibiotics for some <span class="qt1">bacterial</span> infections. For example, you might not need them for many sinus infections or some ear infections. Taking antibiotics when they're not needed won't help you, and they can have side effects. Your health care provider can decide the best treatment for you when you're sick. Don't ask your provider to prescribe an antibiotic for you.</p>Do antibiotics treat viral infections?<p>Antibiotics do not work on viral infections. For example, you shouldn't take antibiotics for:</p><ul><li>Colds and runny noses, even if the mucus is thick, yellow, or green</li><li>Most sore throats (except strep throat)</li><li>Flu</li><li>Most cases of bronchitis</li></ul>What are the side effects of antibiotics?<p>The side effects of antibiotics range from minor to very severe. Some of the common side effects include:</p><ul><li>Rash</li><li>Nausea</li><li>Diarrhea</li><li>Yeast infections</li></ul><p>More serious side effects can include:</p><ul><li>C. diff infections, which cause diarrhea that can lead to severe colon damage and sometimes even death</li><li>Severe and life-threatening allergic reactions</li><li>Antibiotic resistance infections</li></ul><p>Call your health care provider if you develop any side effects while taking your antibiotic.</p>Why is it important to take antibiotics only when they're needed?<p>You should only take antibiotics when they are needed because they can cause side effects and can contribute to Antibiotic resistance infections. Antibiotic resistance happens when the <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> change and become able to resist the effects of an antibiotic. This means that the <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> continue to grow.</p>How do I use antibiotics correctly?<p>When you take antibiotics, it is important that you take them responsibly:</p><ul><li>Always follow the directions carefully. Finish your medicine even if you feel better. If you stop taking them too soon, some <span class="qt1">bacteria</span> may survive and re-infect you.</li><li>Don't save your antibiotics for later.</li><li>Don't share your antibiotic with others.</li><li>Don't take antibiotics prescribed for someone else. This may delay the best treatment for you, make you even sicker, or cause side effects.</li></ul><p>Centers for Disease Control and Prevention</p></content>
